label: Afternoon edition
summary: Keanu, **Wall Street staged its best day since April 2025** on Monday: the Dow rose 3.01% to 49,595.31, the S&P 500 gained 4.73% to 7,237.17 and the Nasdaq jumped 6.51% (CNBC). Nvidia led, up about 31%, after its board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO following a push from Trump (CNBC, Bloomberg, Fox Business). **Congress reacted with bipartisan anger**, and Huang will testify before Senate Banking on Dec. 3 (The Hill, Axios). Anthropic slipped slightly while tech rallied (CNBC). Locally, **king tides peak Wednesday morning** near 8.5 feet, just under the 1983 record, and San Francisco urges avoiding nonessential travel through Wednesday afternoon (CNN, SF Chronicle). Trump used a Justice Department event to attack Newsom's death-row commutations, and Newsom says no one on former death row will leave prison (CNN, Fox News). Democrats head toward a **Dec. 1 vote between Schumer and Van Hollen** (The Hill, Axios). Brent crude fell about 2.8% to near $90 even as Gulf shipping attacks continued (CNBC), and Fed Governor Waller still wants a half-point hike on Dec. 8 to 9 (Bloomberg, CNBC). The FAA still has no confirmed root cause for the Nov. 13 ground stop (Axios). In science, **astronomers may have seen a star swallow its companion** in Andromeda (Space.com, Science News).

stories.title: Both parties push back on Jensen Huang's reinstatement and set a Dec. 3 Senate hearing
stories.summary: Democrats vow investigations and several Republicans object to White House involvement, while the Senate Banking Committee schedules Huang's public testimony.
story: Nvidia's board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO on Monday, Nov. 23, and the reaction in Congress was bipartisan and sharp (Axios, The Hill, CNN). Senate Banking Committee Chairman Tim Scott set an open hearing for Dec. 3 at 10 a.m. ET, titled "Protecting America's AI Advantage: Oversight of U.S. Export Controls." Huang is the only listed witness. The Hill also reports a separate, closed-door House session before then, and a Dec. 10 session with Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.

Huang resigned on Nov. 12 amid a scandal over his ties to a woman who was alleged to be a Chinese spy. The Justice Department has not said whether that allegation is true, and Beijing has rejected it (Fox News, CNN). Nvidia's board said input from senior levels of the U.S. government led it to conclude his return carries no national security risk. Trump told CNBC he spoke with the board directly, and CNN reports Attorney General Todd Blanche told Trump the department has no evidence of wrongdoing by Huang or Nvidia.

Democrats are split between oversight and legislation. Sen. Elizabeth Warren called the move "reckless" and said the administration must explain what input it gave. House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries called it indefensible and tied it to "ironclad" chip export limits in the defense bill, and Sen. Andy Kim asked for classified briefings and sworn testimony (The Hill). Republicans are divided. Rep. Don Bacon said Huang "was compromised and exploited by a Chinese spy," Sen. Pete Ricketts said his behavior does not support reinstatement, and Sen. John Cornyn asked "Based on what?" (The Hill, Washington Examiner). Trump called Huang a "Great Patriot and National Treasure" (Fox Business, National Review).

What it means: the fight now combines a personnel scandal, export controls on AI chips and questions about how much the White House steered a private company's board. Axios reports Democrats plan their own investigations when they take control of Congress next year.
stories.flag: Whether the White House pressed the board, and what exactly the government told it, rests on Trump's own account and Nvidia's statement. No document has been released.
facts: Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO on Monday, Nov. 23, after he resigned Nov. 12.
Senate Banking will hold an open hearing with Huang on Dec. 3 at 10 a.m. ET (The Hill).
Lutnick is separately slated to appear Dec. 10 (The Hill).
Democrats and Republicans have both criticized the decision, for different reasons.
The Justice Department has not determined whether the woman at the center of the scandal was a Chinese spy (Fox News).
stories.left: The strongest progressive case is about accountability and process. A foreign-intelligence concern touched the head of the company that makes the chips at the center of U.S.-China competition, and a president then lobbied the board to bring him back before its own investigation finished. Warren and Kim want sworn testimony and a look at what Lutnick and Bessent knew. Many Democrats also argue export controls should be written into law rather than left to a president who can be moved by market swings, as Trump himself suggested the selloff influenced his view.
stories.right: Conservatives are split, and the split is real. Hawks like Bacon, Ricketts and Gingrich argue that a compromised executive should not run the firm that supplies the world's best AI chips, and that a board bowing to White House pressure sets a bad precedent. Others on the right side with Trump: the Justice Department says it has no evidence of wrongdoing, American AI leadership depends on Nvidia staying strong, and Huang is a proven operator whose absence cost shareholders and the country's tech edge nearly a trillion dollars in a week.
stories.next: Huang's closed House session, then the Dec. 3 Senate Banking hearing at 10 a.m. ET, and Lutnick on Dec. 10.

stories.title: Schumer and Van Hollen head into a Dec. 1 secret ballot with both camps claiming momentum
stories.summary: Schumer says he has the votes and Van Hollen calls the race wide open; most senators have not said publicly how they will vote.
story: Senate Democrats will pick their leader by secret ballot on Dec. 1, and the contest between Chuck Schumer and Chris Van Hollen is still being measured through public statements (The Hill, Axios, Fox News). The Hill's whip list showed 15 senators backing Schumer, five backing Van Hollen and 34 who had not said. A candidate needs 28 votes, though Axios noted the threshold could be 29 depending on Alaska's unresolved Senate race.

Schumer told reporters, "I'm confident I'll be the next leader," and allies predict more than 40 votes, which is their own projection (The Hill). Van Hollen calls himself the underdog but says it is a "wide-open race" and accused Democrats of trying to move the vote up to hurt his chances. Fox News reported both sides claim they can reach 28.

At least six incoming senators, including Abdul El-Sayed, Peggy Flanagan and Annie Andrews, have said they will not support Schumer (The Hill). Because the ballot is secret, senators can vote differently from what they say. Fox News frames the fight as a revolt against Schumer's leadership.
facts: The Senate Democratic leadership vote is a secret ballot on Dec. 1.
The winner needs 28 votes, or 29 if the Alaska race affects the count (Axios).
The Hill's whip list showed 15 for Schumer, five for Van Hollen and 34 undecided.
Six senators-elect have said they will not back Schumer (The Hill).
stories.left: Supporters of change argue Democrats won the midterms and the base wants a fighter who will force limits on the Iran war and challenge the administration harder, with new faces at the top. Defenders of Schumer say experience and relationships matter most heading into a December funding fight and a new majority, and that a messy leadership change could cost leverage on both.
stories.right: Conservative commentators see a party at odds with itself, with its Senate leader weakened less by Republicans than by his own caucus. They argue the fight shows Democrats cannot agree on whether to shut down the government over Iran, and they expect either outcome to push the party further left or leave it divided.
stories.next: The Dec. 1 caucus vote, ten days before the Dec. 11 funding deadline.
stories.blindspot: Found mostly center and right-leaning coverage this pass; no new left-leaning outlet reporting on the count.

stories.title: Trump attacks Newsom's death-row commutations at a Justice Department event
stories.summary: Trump called the commutations a shocking injustice and promised more federal death-penalty pursuits, while Newsom says everyone on former death row will die in prison.
story: President Trump used a Justice Department event on Monday, Nov. 23, to attack California Gov. Gavin Newsom's plan to commute death sentences, calling it "one of the most shocking acts of injustice our country has ever seen" (CNN, Fox News). Relatives of murder victims spoke at the event, and one told Newsom to "Face me." Attorney General Todd Blanche said the department has sought the death penalty 49 times since January 2025, and Trump vowed to seek it for child murderers and speed up federal executions.

Newsom announced on Nov. 5 that he would convert all of California's death sentences to life without parole. The state's fact sheet counted 548 people on death row, while Trump cited 563 (CalMatters, CNN). The change is not yet in effect. Many of the cases need review by the California Supreme Court because they involve people with more than one felony conviction. Fox News, citing the Associated Press, put that number at 382, while other reports describe more than 400, so the count is not settled.

Newsom's office pointed to his earlier letter. In a video he said every person on former death row will die in prison and accused Trump of using pardons to protect wealthy allies. Many California district attorneys object. Orange County DA Todd Spitzer called it "mercy for the wolves," and the California District Attorneys Association opposes it, while the ACLU praised it (Fox News). CNN framed the attack as part of an early 2028 matchup, since both men may run.
stories.flag: The number of commutations that require state Supreme Court approval is reported differently (382 per Fox citing AP; more than 400 in earlier coverage).
stories.blindspot: No center-left explanation of the legal path beyond CNN and CalMatters turned up this pass.
facts: Newsom announced the commutations Nov. 5; none are in effect yet.
The state counted 548 death-row inmates; Trump cited 563.
Blanche said DOJ has sought the death penalty 49 times since January 2025.
Many district attorneys oppose the move; the ACLU supports it.
CNN reports the clash is also a preview of a possible 2028 race.
stories.left: Supporters say California's system has failed for decades: it has executed no one in years, cost billions, and risks killing innocent people, so ending it is both humane and practical. They note the prisoners stay locked up for life, and they see Trump's use of a Justice Department platform to attack a political rival as a misuse of an official setting.
stories.right: Critics say one governor is overriding the voters and hundreds of individual jury verdicts, including those for child killers, and that victims' families are being told their cases no longer matter. A National Review writer would add that clemency on this scale, done in a lame-duck period without a hearing for each case, undermines public trust in the justice system whatever one thinks of capital punishment.
stories.next: Whether prosecutors file a lawsuit, and the state Supreme Court's review of the commutations.

stories.title: Near-record king tides and a storm hit the Bay Area Tuesday and Wednesday
stories.summary: A coastal flood warning runs through Thanksgiving, with the highest water forecast Wednesday morning and San Francisco urging residents to avoid nonessential travel.
story: The Bay Area is bracing for a storm that arrives with some of the highest tides in decades (CNN, SF Chronicle, NBC News). A coastal flood warning runs from early Monday through Thanksgiving Day, with the worst flooding risk around each morning's high tide and the highest water on Wednesday, Nov. 25. San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie asked residents to avoid nonessential travel from Monday afternoon through Wednesday afternoon, and Marin officials made a similar request for 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. Tuesday through Thursday.

Forecasters expected water levels near 8.5 feet at Wednesday morning's high tide, inches short of the 1983 record of 8.82 feet (CNN). The Posey Tube between Alameda and Oakland is closed from 8 p.m. Sunday to 5 p.m. Friday, and the Baylands Nature Preserve in Palo Alto is closed Monday through Saturday. Rain forecasts vary. Some outlets say a quarter-inch to an inch through Wednesday, while others say up to 3 inches in the North Bay.

For Fremont, the local forecast shows a 74% chance of rain on both Tuesday and Wednesday. None of the coverage found addresses the Fremont shoreline directly, so check National Weather Service and City of Fremont alerts for bayside areas. Even higher king tides are expected around Christmas week and in January.
stories.flag: The coverage found did not mention Fremont or the south bay shoreline specifically.
facts: A coastal flood warning runs from Monday through Thanksgiving Day, with Wednesday's morning tide the highest.
Forecast peak of about 8.5 feet is inches below the 1983 record of 8.82 feet (CNN).
San Francisco asks residents to avoid nonessential travel from Monday afternoon to Wednesday afternoon.
Fremont has a 74% chance of rain Tuesday and Wednesday (Open-Meteo).
stories.left: Climate-focused observers point to these tides as a preview of sea-level rise on a low-lying bay, arguing the region needs faster funding for shoreline protection, transit resilience and managed retreat in the worst-hit places.
stories.right: Skeptics of the climate framing say king tides are a predictable astronomical event, and the real question is whether local governments maintained levees, drainage and emergency plans that are paid for by existing budgets before asking for more money.
stories.next: Updated National Weather Service forecasts; the peak tide is Wednesday morning, Nov. 25.
stories.blindspot: Covered mainly by center and left-leaning outlets; no right-leaning coverage found.

stories.title: California's budget analyst warns an AI-linked market crash could mean $35 billion annual deficits
stories.summary: The Legislative Analyst says a milder slowdown would still open a $2 billion gap in 2027-28, and the state lacks reserves for a crash.
story: California's nonpartisan Legislative Analyst's Office warned that an abrupt market crash tied to AI could push the state's annual deficit to about $35 billion by fiscal 2028-29, and the state would not have enough reserves to cover it (CalMatters, KQED). A milder stock-market slowdown next year would produce a smaller $2 billion deficit by 2027-28, rising to about $15 billion the following year.

The warning lands as Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra prepares to take office in January and inherits a budget shortfall (KQED). The state's revenue leans heavily on income taxes from high earners and capital gains, which makes it sensitive to tech stock swings. Monday's 4.7% S&P 500 rally does not remove that exposure, since the analyst's scenarios are about a sustained downturn.
CalMatters also notes that Republicans hold just one in six seats in the Legislature after the election, which leaves Democrats with sole responsibility for any fix.
facts: The LAO scenario of a sudden crash points to a $35 billion annual deficit by fiscal 2028-29.
A milder slowdown would mean about $2 billion in 2027-28 and about $15 billion in 2028-29.
The analyst says the state would lack the reserves to fill a gap that large.
Becerra takes office in January (CalMatters).
stories.left: Progressives say the numbers show why California needs a steadier revenue base, such as higher taxes on the largest fortunes and corporations, and why safety-net programs should be protected from a cyclical downturn that would hit working families hardest.
stories.right: Conservatives argue the state has spent as if the AI boom would last forever, grown ongoing programs and built a structural gap before any crash. They want spending restraint, a larger rainy-day fund and less dependence on a handful of high earners and tech firms.
stories.next: The Department of Finance forecast and Becerra's first budget proposal in January.
stories.blindspot: Only center and left-leaning outlets turned up; no right-leaning coverage found.

stories.title: Oil slips on rising Middle East supply even as attacks on Gulf shipping continue
stories.summary: Brent fell about 2.8% Monday while the Houthis claimed a strike on a Saudi refinery and shipping was hit near Hormuz over the weekend.
story: Oil prices fell Monday as traders weighed more Middle East supply and the restart of a Libyan pipeline against continuing attacks (CNBC). Later in the session Brent futures were down $2.58, or 2.8%, near $89.99 a barrel. Earlier in the morning Brent was around $91.97, so the figures differ by time of day.

The Iran-aligned Houthi movement said it attacked a Saudi Arabian oil refinery, and the UK Maritime Trade Operations reported multiple attacks on shipping in the Gulf and near the Strait of Hormuz over the weekend (CNBC). PVM's Tamas Varga said Iranian attacks on ships in the strait are taking their toll. The Houthi claim was not independently confirmed in the report.

JPMorgan expects oil futures to drop to the high $70s in the first half of 2027 because of an expected supply surplus from higher production outside Iran (CNBC). The WTI figure in the market table is $82.36, from the morning data feed.
stories.flag: The Houthi refinery claim is the group's own and was not independently confirmed in the coverage found.
stories.blindspot: Only CNBC's coverage turned up for this update; no left- or right-leaning outlet reporting found.
facts: Brent fell $2.58, or 2.8%, to about $89.99 later Monday (CNBC).
UKMTO reported multiple attacks on shipping in the Gulf and near Hormuz over the weekend.
The Houthis said they attacked a Saudi refinery.
JPMorgan sees futures falling to the high $70s in the first half of 2027.
stories.left: Critics of the war argue the continued attacks show military pressure has not secured shipping lanes, and that falling prices reflect market resilience rather than any strategic win. They want Congress to set limits and a diplomatic path.
stories.right: Supporters argue that the U.S. campaign has degraded Iran's ability to disrupt supply, that exports are recovering and prices are down from $110 in October, and that attacks on tankers show why pressure on Tehran should continue.
stories.next: Weekend shipping incident reports from UKMTO and Wednesday's U.S. crude inventory data.

stories.title: After the Trump-Xi-Putin summit, a nuclear-risk pledge but no Ukraine breakthrough
stories.summary: The three leaders pledged a dialogue on nuclear risks, and Zelensky says Putin did not get a division of influence.
story: The three-way summit in Shenzhen produced a joint declaration that "a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought," and a pledge to hold a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks, with no binding arms cuts or timetable (The Hill, NPR). The declaration made no mention of Ukraine. Trump rated the meeting "12 out of 10" (Fox News) and told skeptical Europeans that Putin wants to end the war (Axios).

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky had warned against a "Yalta 2" carve-up of influence, and afterward said Putin did not get one and that the summit turned out badly for Russia (Fox News). Special envoy Jared Kushner said Putin is comfortable with NATO-like security guarantees for Ukraine, though any U.S. commitment would need Congress (The Hill).

U.S. reaction is mixed. Sen. Thom Tillis accused Xi and Putin of theft and death, and Democrats warned Trump against cozying up to them (The Hill). NPR's assessment is that the meeting resulted only in an agreement to keep talking.
facts: The joint declaration reaffirmed that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought.
No binding arms reductions or timetable were announced.
Ukraine was not mentioned in the declaration.
Zelensky said Putin did not get a "Yalta 2."
stories.left: Critics say Trump gave two adversaries a platform and a photo-op while Ukraine got nothing, and that a pledge without a timetable is a statement, not a treaty. They want sanctions pressure on Russia and a seat for Kyiv in any deal.
stories.right: Supporters say direct talks with Xi and Putin on nuclear risk are overdue and better than escalation, and credit Trump with keeping Europe at the table. More hawkish conservatives, such as Tillis, remain wary of warmth toward both leaders.
stories.next: Whether Washington and Moscow schedule the promised nuclear-risk dialogue, and any new Ukraine negotiating round.

stories.title: Fed's Waller says a half-point December hike should be considered as markets price a quarter point
stories.summary: October inflation ran hot and officials expect more hikes, but traders see a quarter-point move as the base case.
story: Fed Governor Christopher Waller said Nov. 18 that the Fed should consider a half-point rate hike at its Dec. 8 to 9 meeting, after he said Nov. 10 that a quarter-point was likely (Bloomberg, CNBC). He warned a smaller move could put the Fed's credibility at risk and that the Fed may need to "shock" markets. He is the only central banker to say so publicly. Traders still price a quarter-point hike as the base case, with a very small chance of a half-point (CNBC).

The trigger was October consumer prices, which rose 0.4%, more than expected (CNBC). The September PCE data showed headline inflation at 3.6% annually and core at 3.1% (CNBC). Minutes of the October meeting show officials expect more hikes and worry about AI's effect on inflation. Odds favor another increase in January and perhaps one more before the end of 2027.
The 10-year Treasury yield was 4.91% in the morning data feed. A larger hike matters for the stock rally, since higher rates weigh on the AI stocks that bounced Monday.
stories.blindspot: Only center and financial outlets turned up; no left- or right-leaning coverage found.
facts: Waller said Nov. 18 the Fed should consider a half-point hike on Dec. 8 to 9.
October CPI rose 0.4%, above forecasts (CNBC).
September PCE inflation was 3.6% for headline and 3.1% for core.
The October minutes show officials expect more hikes (CNBC).
stories.left: Critics worry the Fed is tightening into a market that has just fallen about 10%, with a possible AI bust and rising bankruptcies ahead, and that a supersized hike risks needless job losses. Some argue AI-driven price effects call for supply-side policy rather than higher rates.
stories.right: Conservatives point to 3.6% PCE inflation and a hot CPI as proof the Fed waited too long, and want a credible, forceful response now. They argue that delaying costs more later and that markets should adjust to the reality that rates are rising.
stories.next: The Dec. 8 to 9 Fed meeting and the November CPI report.

stories.title: Stocks surge in their best day since April 2025 as Nvidia reinstates Huang
stories.summary: The Nasdaq jumped 6.51%, the S&P 500 4.73% and the Dow 3.01%, led by chip stocks, though strategists are split on whether it lasts.
story: Wall Street rebounded sharply Monday. The Dow rose 1,447.98 points, or 3.01%, to 49,595.31, the S&P 500 gained 4.73% to 7,237.17, and the Nasdaq Composite jumped 6.51% to 24,089.56, according to CNBC. The S&P 500 and Nasdaq each had their best day since April 2025. The gains followed a week that left all three major averages in correction territory, down about 10% from their highs.

Nvidia led the move. It rose about 31% after announcing Jensen Huang's return as CEO, and CNBC and Bloomberg describe a rally across AI-linked and chip stocks (CNBC, Bloomberg, Fox Business). Anthropic, which listed last Thursday, did not join the rally and ended slightly lower (CNBC).

Strategists are divided on durability. CNBC reports that many traders think the rebound could fail before it recovers last week's losses, and the Fed's Dec. 8 to 9 meeting with a rate hike expected remains a risk. Dell reports Tuesday after the close, and CNBC calls it a test of AI demand.
The quote table below was last updated Monday morning and shows Friday's closing prices, so it does not reflect these gains. The closing figures here come from CNBC.
stories.flag: The market table's index and stock prices are from the data feed's morning snapshot (Friday closes). Monday's closing figures are CNBC's and are not in the table.
facts: The S&P 500 and Nasdaq had their best day since April 2025.
Nvidia rose about 31% on the day; Bloomberg said it was up as much as 35% intraday.
All three major averages had been in correction before Monday.
stories.why: The rally shows how much the market's direction now hangs on one company and one executive. A reversal in confidence in Nvidia, or a bigger Fed hike, could erase the gain as fast as it came.
stories.next: Dell earnings Tuesday after the close, and the Fed meeting on Dec. 8 to 9.

stories.title: FAA ground-stop investigation: a router surge is the trigger, but the root cause is still unknown
stories.summary: Investigators point to a router in Arkansas and a second one in Texas, and the FAA has paused router installations.
story: The FAA's nationwide ground stop on Friday, Nov. 13 began at 3:54 p.m. ET and ended at 8:15 p.m. Investigators point to a new router at an El Dorado, Arkansas facility that produced a surge of roughly 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds, destabilizing the agency's telecom network (Axios, AvWeb).

The central open question is why a second router in Amarillo, Texas, also misbehaved when the two sites are more than 500 miles apart (ABC7). Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said officials are examining whether the cause was an installation error by contractor L3Harris or faulty equipment. The routers are Juniper devices, and Hewlett Packard Enterprise said its equipment "was working as configured."

The FAA paused router installations and disabled a broadcasting function on about 60 similar routers. Reporting said there is no indication of a cyberattack. The newest reporting found is from about Nov. 17, and it names no confirmed root cause.
stories.flag: No confirmed root cause as of the latest reporting found (about Nov. 17).
facts: The ground stop ran from 3:54 p.m. to 8:15 p.m. ET on Friday, Nov. 13.
A router in El Dorado, Arkansas generated about 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds.
A second router in Amarillo, Texas, more than 500 miles away, also misbehaved.
The FAA paused router installs and disabled a feature on about 60 similar routers.
stories.why: This is a case study in how one misbehaving device can cascade through a legacy network, and why aviation's modernization depends on testing upgrades under real conditions before wide rollout.
stories.next: The FAA's root-cause finding and the timeline for resuming router installations.

stories.title: Anthropic launches Claude Ship, agents that review, fix and approve code changes
stories.summary: The suite adds beta agents for fixing failing checks and approving routine changes, aimed at the bottleneck of reviewing AI-written code.
story: Anthropic introduced Claude Ship on Monday, a suite of agents for reviewing code, fixing it and approving routine changes (TechCrunch). It includes Code Review, which is already generally available, and two beta agents: PR Steward, which handles failing CI checks, merge conflicts and Code Review feedback, and Claude Approvals, which applies an approval policy a team writes in plain language as a file in its repository.

Anthropic suggests running the approvals feature in observe-only mode first, limiting the rollout to one repository and setting monthly spending caps. It is rolling out to Team and Enterprise plans for GitHub repositories (TechCrunch). The launch targets a bottleneck: AI agents now produce so much code that review and approval lag behind.

Code Review first launched in March as a research preview. At that time reviews cost about $15 to $25 each and ran about 20 minutes, and Anthropic said the share of pull requests with substantive comments rose from 16% to 54% in testing, which is the company's own measurement (TechCrunch, Anthropic).
stories.flag: Detail comes mainly from TechCrunch and Anthropic, and the performance figures are the company's own. Anthropic also makes the AI model that helps produce this feed.
facts: Claude Ship launched Monday, Nov. 23.
It bundles Code Review plus beta PR Steward and Claude Approvals agents.
Approval policies are written in natural language in a repository file.
It is available to Team and Enterprise plans on GitHub.
stories.why: If agents can safely approve low-risk changes, the human review bottleneck eases. The risk is that AI checks AI, so teams should keep humans on high-risk code and watch false approvals.
stories.next: Early user reports on false approvals and cost once the beta reaches more teams.

stories.title: Astronomers may have watched a giant star swallow its companion for the first time
stories.summary: A Nature paper describes a red giant in Andromeda that brightened for years as a smaller star spiraled inside it.
story: Astronomers report what may be the first direct observation of a star engulfing a companion, in a Nature paper published Nov. 18 and led by Viraj Karambelkar of Columbia University (Space.com, Science News). The red giant, cataloged as WNTR23bzdiq and nicknamed "Big Bao," sits in the Andromeda galaxy, about 2.5 million light-years away. It is about seven times the Sun's mass and about 350 times wider.

Its companion, "Little Bao," had about 70% of the Sun's mass. As it spiraled through the giant's outer gas, friction produced heat and light, which explains why the giant brightened for roughly seven years from about 2018 before erupting (Space.com, IFLScience). Accounts differ on the eruption date, with one saying October 2025 and others saying late 2025.

Heavy dust now hides the system, so astronomers cannot see what is left. Researchers say mergers of smaller stars have been seen before, but not this common-envelope process in a giant (Nature Asia press release). The paper is titled "An Inspiral of a Star Inside a Common Envelope with its Giant Companion," in Nature 659, 628-633 (2026).
stories.flag: Accounts differ on the eruption date (October 2025 versus late 2025). The description of the final state is limited by dust.
facts: The paper appeared in Nature on Nov. 18, led by Viraj Karambelkar (Columbia).
The red giant is about 7 solar masses and 350 times the Sun's width.
The companion had about 0.7 solar masses.
The system is in Andromeda, about 2.5 million light-years away.
Dust prevents direct observation of the remnant.
stories.why: Common-envelope events are thought to create close binaries, including systems that later merge as black holes or neutron stars and produce gravitational waves. Watching one live tests models that were mostly theory.
stories.next: Follow-up infrared observations as the dust clears; no date has been announced.

stories.title: Voyager 1 passed one light-day from Earth but has sent no science data since Nov. 14
stories.summary: Ground antennas still detect Voyager's carrier signal, but it carries no data, and NASA says the flight data system is the likely cause.
story: Voyager 1 reached one light-day from Earth this month, a first for any spacecraft, but the mission team has seen no science or engineering data since Nov. 14 (NASA, Nature). Ground antennas still detect the carrier signal, which carries no data. NASA's view is that the likely cause is the onboard flight data system that packages the data.

The team has seen something like this before. A similar problem began in November 2023 and was fixed in June 2024. If the fix works, Voyager 1 will keep transmitting from its two remaining science instruments, a magnetometer and a plasma wave detector (Space.com).
Project manager Suzanne Dodd said she is confident science data will flow again soon, though no update has been published since the milestone announcement and none is scheduled.
stories.flag: I found no NASA update after the Nov. 18 mission blog post.
facts: Voyager 1 hit one light-day from Earth in November 2026.
No science or engineering data has been received since Nov. 14.
The carrier signal is still detected.
A similar fault lasted from November 2023 to June 2024.
stories.why: Voyager 1 is one of only two human-made objects in interstellar space, and its two remaining instruments make direct measurements there. Each outage risks a permanent loss on a spacecraft nearly 50 years old.
stories.next: NASA's next status update on the data fault; none is scheduled.

stories.title: Nvidia's stock jumps about 31% as the board brings Jensen Huang back
stories.summary: Nvidia regained nearly $1 trillion in market value in its best day since 2003, with analysts upgrading and questions about the SEC probe still open.
story: Nvidia shares rose about 31.5% on Monday after the board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO, president and director (CNBC, Axios). Nvidia gained back nearly $1 trillion in market value and posted its best day since May 2003. Bloomberg said the stock was up as much as 35% to 37% intraday. Analysts upgraded the stock, and Oppenheimer's $250 price target is roughly double Nvidia's prior close (CNBC).

Huang resigned Nov. 12 after reports of his ties to a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy. Trump said he spoke with the board and that the sell-off probably influenced his support for Huang's return (CNBC, Bloomberg). Nvidia's board said it had input from senior government officials that his return carries no national security risk, and said its own export-control investigation continues (Fox Business).

The Wall Street Journal reported the SEC is running a civil investigation into whether Nvidia's disclosures were accurate. Neither Nvidia nor the SEC has confirmed it. California Attorney General Rob Bonta said his office is looking into the matter. Strategists are split on whether the rebound holds, and Warren says Huang and Nvidia still owe Congress answers on export controls.
stories.flag: The SEC investigation is reported by the Wall Street Journal and not confirmed by Nvidia or the SEC; its scope is unverified.
facts: Nvidia stock rose about 31.5% Monday, its best day since May 2003 (CNBC).
The board reinstated Huang as CEO, president and director.
Nvidia regained nearly $1 trillion in market value.
The WSJ reported an SEC civil probe; neither Nvidia nor the SEC has confirmed it.
Huang is scheduled to testify in the Senate Dec. 3.
stories.why: Nvidia is the AI trade's bellwether, so its leadership drama drives the Nasdaq. The company also sits at the center of U.S. policy on chip exports to China.
stories.left: Progressives argue the episode shows a company too important to fail being managed by presidential phone call, and want sworn testimony and enforceable export rules.
stories.right: Conservatives who support the move say the board and Justice Department reviewed the facts and a proven CEO should lead a strategic company; hawkish conservatives say the unresolved China and export questions mean he should not.
stories.next: Huang's Senate Banking hearing on Dec. 3 and any SEC or California action.

stories.title: Anthropic slips slightly Monday while the rest of tech rallies
stories.summary: The stock rose in premarket trading but ended a little lower, after a volatile first week following its record IPO.
story: Anthropic's shares rose about 4.5% in premarket trading Monday but ended the day a little lower, one CNBC report put the decline at 1.43%, while another had it down about 3% in the afternoon (CNBC, Fox Business). The stock was among the few names that did not join Monday's rally.

The company raised a record $93.5 billion in its IPO, priced at $83 a share against a marketed range of $70 to $78, which valued it near $1.5 trillion (CNBC). It opened at $111.50 on Thursday, gained 17% in its debut and closed down 8.5% on Friday.
The broader selloff in AI stocks last week complicated the debut. Lockup release dates, once the company publishes them, are the next scheduled test of investor confidence.
stories.flag: Monday's exact move differs by report because of timing. Anthropic makes Claude, the AI model that helps produce this feed.
facts: The IPO priced at $83, above the $70 to $78 range.
It raised a record $93.5 billion (CNBC).
Shares gained 17% on debut day and fell 8.5% on Friday.
Monday's close was down slightly, with reports of 1.43% and about 3%.
stories.why: The IPO is a test of whether public investors will pay frontier-lab valuations after a sharp AI selloff. Its trading will shape how other AI companies approach going public.
stories.left: Critics worry public ownership will pull a safety-focused lab toward growth and short-term returns, and say a $1.5 trillion valuation shows how concentrated AI power has become.
stories.right: Supporters see a market validating American AI leadership and giving ordinary investors access to the boom. Skeptics say valuations assume a boom the Fed and rising rates may not allow.
stories.next: Dell's earnings Tuesday and later lockup release dates once Anthropic publishes them.

stories.title: Newsom's expert panel recommends an emergency AI shutdown power, and a special session is possible
stories.summary: The package also calls for independent auditors and expanded incident reporting, and the governor has not ruled out acting before Dec. 7.
story: Gov. Gavin Newsom released recommendations from an expert panel that include letting state officials order an immediate emergency shutdown, or "kill switch," of AI systems they judge dangerous (CalMatters, KQED). The package also calls for independent auditors who could cost companies their licenses and for broader safety-incident reporting. The report covers only catastrophic risk, not harms such as discrimination or job loss.

Newsom has said his team is preparing bills and has not ruled out a special session, but he wants to be sensitive to Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra, who takes office Jan. 4. A special session before the new Legislature convenes on Dec. 7 has not been called (KQED, SF Chronicle).

Republican candidate Steve Hilton called the kill switch "a gimmick" but said he would convene a similar panel. Becerra's office did not say whether he would adopt the recommendations, and Sen. Scott Wiener is expected to push AI safety bills after he is sworn in.
stories.flag: Whether a special session will be called is not confirmed.
facts: The panel recommends letting officials order an emergency AI shutdown.
It also proposes independent auditors and expanded incident reporting.
The report covers catastrophic risk only.
No special session has been called.
stories.why: California is the home of most leading AI labs, so its rules can become national in practice. A state shutdown power would be the first of its kind.
stories.left: Supporters argue frontier labs cannot be trusted to police themselves and that a narrow, enforceable emergency power is a modest backstop. Labor leaders want broader protections.
stories.right: Critics say a kill switch is vague, hard to use on distributed models and could push companies out of the state, and that state rules duplicate federal oversight. Hilton called it a gimmick.
stories.next: Whether Newsom calls a special session before Dec. 7, and the first bills in the new session.

briefs: The U.S. lost its measles elimination status Nov. 17, with more than 5,400 cases and about 10 deaths this year, and CDC Director Erica Schwartz said vaccination, not the designation, protects people (NPR, NBC News, CNN).
OpenAI announced GPT-6.2 Astra for professional work and GPT-6.2 Sol as its everyday model on Nov. 17, and says both use fewer output tokens on hard tasks; the claims are OpenAI's (Bloomberg).
Amazon is buying Decart's AI optimization technology for $7.5 billion as it prepares to sell Trainium chips (TechCrunch).
JWST found the oldest known pair of black-hole-powered quasars, separated by about 18,100 light-years (Space.com).
Trump paused the Army's planned detonation of explosive chemicals at an Iowa site, which had been set for Wednesday (CNN, NBC News).
Dell reports Tuesday after the close and is read as a test of AI demand (CNBC).
